zones.name: Northwest Zone
zones.html:
NW Zone -

  • Fall salmon fishing slowed on Nehalem, Tillamook, and Nestucca bays this past week following the rain. All basins are still producing a few Chinook and coho salmon. Wild coho retention is now closed on these basins, no wild coho adults may be retained as of Oct. 28. Angling for hatchery coho is still open and there are a few hatchery coho coming through Tillamook and Nehalem bays. See the regulation updates online at Fall Coastal Salmon Management for details on seasons and bag limits.
  • Fall Chinook are entering the lower reaches of North Coast Rivers the past week with the Trask and Wilson Rivers being the most productive for anglers.
  • The Trask River, North Fork Nehalem River, and Lower Columbia Tributaries should have hatchery coho arriving with the recent rains, but fishing has remained slow although a few fish are being caught.
  • The Kilchis and Miami Rivers have catch and release only fisheries for chum salmon and there are probably some showing up in the lower reaches of those rivers. Anglers are encouraged to use good ethics and avoid disturbing actively spawning fish or redds (spawning nest in the gravel) and avoid snagging.

The Nestucca and Wilson Rivers still have summer steelhead available, mostly in the upper reaches. Fall can be a good time to target these fish that have been holding most of the summer, as the dropping water temperatures and fall rains can get them more active and willing to bite.

  • Trout stocking has been completed in North Coast lakes for the year, but there are still hold-over trout available to catch in many of the lakes.
  • Fall Chinook fishing has slowed in the Siletz, Alsea, Siuslaw, Yaquina and Salmon rivers. Chinook are spawning in many systems and anglers are asked to not disturb fish on redds as they are especially susceptible during low flow conditions.
  • Wild coho retention is open in the Siletz and Yaquina rivers through Nov 7. Refer to Fall Coastal Salmon Management for more information on season outlines and bag limits.
  • Siltcoos and Tahkenitch lakes are open for wild coho retention. Some early fish may be around, but the majority won't show up until we receive some measurable rain.

zones.name: Southwest Zone
zones.html:
Weekend's Best Bets

SW Zone –

  • Try some late season trout fishing on either Garrison or Floras Lakes. Garrison Lake usually has some fairly good numbers of trout that carry over from the spring stockings.
  • Anglers are still picking up fall chinook trolling the Chetco River estuary.
  • Empire, Saunders, and Butterfield Lakes were stocked recently with legal trout.
  • Diamond Lake is still producing some nice rainbows, along with catch and release brown trout and tiger trout.

zones.name: Willamette Zone
zones.html:
Willamette Zone -

  • Coho salmon can be found throughout the North Santiam as far up as Packsaddle Park. Spinners such as Blue Fox are usually effective but bobbers and eggs will work as well. Best sections currently are from Green's Bridge down to Jefferson, as well as further down into the mainstem of the Santiam River.
  • Walleye fishing has been good along stretches of the Willamette River from Peoria downstream to Independence. A jet boat is the best option for getting at fish on some stretches, but fishing in 12-18 feet of water, especially trolling a worm spinner downstream a little faster than the currant has been netting some good-sized walleye.

zones.name: Central Zone
zones.html:
Central Zone -

  • Following trophy trout stockings, the Fall River has been fishing exceptionally well.
  • Pine Nursery Pond in Bend was recently stocked with rainbow and brown trout.
  • Reports of consistent trout fishing on the lower Deschutes around the Trout Creek area.

zones.name: Southeast Zone
zones.html:
SE Zone –

  • Fishing for trout at Lost Creek Reservoir.
  • Malheur Reservoir – great for Rainbow Trout from 10-22". Common sizes are 12-16" but we captured fish up to 22" in our sampling this week. We also fly-fished it in the evening and morning and had catches of 10+ trout/hr. We saw people having success trolling and bank fishing with bait as well. Water temperatures were in the mid 50's. You can launch a boat from the boat ramp. Water is up to the old school bus. If you know you know.
  • Yellowjacket Reservoir – Great fishing without a crowd! We sampled last week and found fish from 8-18" with a common size of 12-15". We fished leech patterns under an indicator midday and had non-stop action. Water temperatures are in the mid-50's here, too.
  • Many streams are closed to protect spawning Redband Trout and Chinook Salmon in the Klamath Basin. Your best bets are Klamath Lake and Klamath River below Keno Dam for Redband Trout.
  • Yellow perch angling still might be good in Lake of the Woods, Gerber Reservoir and Upper Klamath Lake near Rocky Point.
  • Big Brown Trout are cruising the shoreline at Miller Lake.
  • Crappie angling has been excellent at Dog Lake recently.

zones.name: Northeast Zone
zones.html:
NE Zone -

  • Tiger Muskies are hungry and aggressive at Phillips Reservoir. Try your luck before winter sets in. Water temperature is prime right now in the low 50°F. Fishing should remain hot until water temps drop below 45°F. As a bonus, the low water levels will concentrate fish and may make catching fish easier.
  • Coho fishing has been great on the lower Umatilla River. Expect fishing to remain good into November. Summer steelhead are also present and will become more prominent as the season progresses.
  • Anglers are catching steelhead in both the Grande Ronde and Imnaha Rivers. Focus lower on both rivers this time of year.
  • Kokanee anglers are finding bright fish on the north end of Wallowa Lake. These fish are smaller in size as many larger fish are spawning at the other end of the lake. Kinney Lake was stocked for the winter with trout.

zones.name: Columbia River Zone
zones.html:
Columbia Fishing

November 5, 2026

Current and upcoming fishing opportunities:

Angling for coho has been winding down, but some anglers have still been catching fish around the mouth of the Klickitat River.

Announcements

For the latest regulations, including in-season changes see the fishing regulation update page.

2026 Spring-Summer-Fall Forecasts

Fish consumption advisories

The Oregon Health Authority has issued consumption guidelines for parts of the Columbia River due to high levels of mercury and/or PCBs. Fish with these chemicals look, act, smell and taste like any other fish, so caution is important.

  • Bonneville Dam fish advisory
  • Safe fish choices for pregnancy and young children

Sign up for the latest information on boater access

Marine Board's Opportunities and Access Report incorporates information from federal and state agencies, local facility operators and fellow boaters to provide up-to-date information so boaters can decide where to recreate and what to expect this season. Subscribe to receive email updates.

Click here to find Columbia River regulation updates for salmon, steelhead, shad and sturgeon.

SALMON, STEELHEAD, AND SHAD

The lower Columbia creel program has ended for the year and will resume in February 2027. The creel program above Bonneville will continue for a couple more weeks.

B10: Weekly checking showed two coho released for six boats (16 anglers).

Lower Columbia River: Weekly checking showed four coho kept and one jack Chinook released for eight boats (21 anglers); and no catch for five bank anglers.

Bonneville Dam to McNary Dam: Weekly checking showed 89 coho and two jack coho kept, and 13 Chinook and two coho released for 45 boats (123 anglers); and no catch for two bank anglers.

STURGEON

Lower Columbia River: No report.

Bonneville Dam to McNary Dam: Weekly checking showed one legal sized and one over-legal sized white sturgeon released for one boat (two anglers).

WALLEYE

Lower Columbia River (below Bonneville Dam): Weekly checking showed no catch for one bank angler. Bonneville Dam to McNary Dam: Weekly checking showed four walleye kept for six boats (10 anglers).

zones.name: Snake River Zone
zones.html:
Snake Zone –

  • Fall can be one of the best times of the year to fish for smallmouth and crappie as they stock up on forage for the winter. Look for these fish in shallow areas as they move closer to baitfish that are seeking warmer water temperatures near the surface of the reservoirs.
  • Updated changes to salmon and steelhead bag limits adjusted for Snake River started Sept 23. See the regulation updates page for more information.

zones.name: Marine Zone
zones.html:
MARINE FISHING

November 5, 2026

Announcements

As of Jan 1, 2026, an Ocean Endorsement is needed for most recreational anglers fishing in the ocean. Check the Ocean Endorsement page for more information.

Report unusual fish and ocean conditions

Have you encountered unusual fish or ocean conditions off the Oregon Coast this year? With warm El Niño waters pushing up the coast, we're starting to see unusual tropical visitors migrating north! Report your on-the-water observations to CaCurrent.Observations@noaa.gov (more information available here). Your observations are critical to understanding how changing ocean conditions affect what we see offshore.

Saltwater News Bulletins

Be among the first to know about in-season changes! You can subscribe to receive emails and text message alerts for marine topics that interest you. It's easy to unsubscribe at any time. Your contact information will remain confidential. Three different lists of interests to ocean enthusiasts are available: bottomfish, halibut and ocean salmon.

Bottomfish

A few reminders

  • Visit the sport bottomfish seasons page to see what's new for 2026.
  • Retention of quillback rockfish and yelloweye rockfish remains prohibited.
  • Cabezon is prohibited from Jan 1 through June 30.

Port by port reports for the week beginning Oct 26:

Depoe Bay: Landings averaged 2.2 rockfish per angler, with mostly black, canary, and yellowtail rockfishes landed. Lingcod catches were good at 2 fish per angler.

Newport: Anglers landed 2.75 rockfish per person, mostly black, deacon, and yellowtail rockfishes were observed. Lingcod was good at 1.4 fish per angler.

Charleston: Anglers landed 3.8 rockfish on average, consisting of mainly black rockfish. Lingcod landings were 1.4 fish per angler.

Brookings: Anglers caught 3 rockfish on average; mainly black rockfish were landed. Lingcod was good at 1.7 fish per angler.

The offshore long-leader fishery gives anglers an opportunity to catch more fish and to distribute effort away from nearshore species. Learn more about gear and the fishery.

Bottomfish fishing resources:

  • What can I keep and how many? Keep up with in-season regulation changes.
  • Know what you've caught with some helpful rockfish identification tips (including online quizzes and video).
  • Waypoints for fathom lines and other restricted areas.

Ocean salmon

Recreational ocean salmon fishing is now closed in all Oregon ocean areas. Season options for 2026 will be proposed in March.

Ocean salmon fishing resources:

  • Keep track of where salmon catch and quotas are at north of Cape Falcon and south of Cape Falcon
  • See the ocean salmon regulations in either a time and area graphic view or as a map

Pacific halibut

The Pacific halibut fishing season is now closed for the remainder of 2025. Season options for 2026 will be proposed in mid-February.

See Pacific halibut season dates or visit the sport halibut page for more information.

Shore and estuary fishing

Daily bag limits, seasons and licensing requirements for shore-based anglers are the same as for boat-based anglers.

There are plenty of rocky or sandy fishing sites up and down the coast where shore anglers can drop a line for saltwater fish. Read about how and where

Lingcod and many other bottomfish species are available year-round to shore anglers fishing in rocky areas. A common setup for lingcod is a jig head with a rubber swim bait – it's simple but effective. Also pack a measuring device for lingcod: the minimum legal size is 22 inches.

Surfperch are available in the surf year-round along sandy beaches and rocky shores, with the best fishing (and safest fishing) occurring when swells are small. Find surfperch and other learn to fish workshops and events here.

Want more opportunities that don't include a boat? Check out the crabbing and clamming recreation report for updates on crabs, clams, mussels and more!

When fishing from shore or inside estuaries and bays, it is important to check the tide. Many fish that swim into estuaries and bays, including salmon, surfperch, and Pacific herring, tend to come in with the tide. Catch of these species is more likely to occur closer to slack tide. Additionally, the accessibility of some areas can be completely dependent on the tide. Do not allow the incoming tide to become a safety issue.
